Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

last thursday evening i went to the cedar bench workshop, a small woodworking makerspace in the old freight depot on mason street. i was there for their monthly member meeting, which started at six thirty in the room behind the tool library. rain was tapping on the high windows, and people kept leaving wet jackets on the backs of chairs. there were eleven of us by the time mara, the coordinator, began. a long maple board was being used as the meeting table, with a coffee ring near one end and a row of pencil marks that nobody seemed to mind.

mara started with the usual shop update, but she had put a few things on paper because, as she said, “we keep having the same conversation and then forgetting which part we agreed to talk about.” the dust collector was running loudly again, mostly when the wide-belt sander was on. tom had checked the outside vent and found a strip of loose mesh, but he had not opened the motor housing. mara said she was not asking anyone to fix it during the meeting, only to decide who could look at it with her on saturday. dev volunteered, as long as they first checked the manual, since he had never worked on that model.

the next discussion was about the beginner bench area. two new members had tried to use it on monday and found the clamps mixed in with the hand planes. the room itself is narrow, so there was disagreement about whether a second rack would make things easier or leave too little walking space. jo thought a wall rack could work if it sat beside the sharpening station, while leah said that spot was already awkward when people carried long boards through. nobody measured the space at the meeting. instead, they agreed to take a tape measure and a piece of cardboard over there before ordering anything. that was a proposal, not a purchase decision, mara pointed out.

1. items people wanted to keep in view

- the cabinet key stays on the hook by the sign-in clipboard, rather than in the drawer where it had been found twice.
- the maple offcuts are for member projects, but anything shorter than six inches should go in the kindling bin unless someone labels it for a specific use.
- safety glasses are still required at the lathe, even for a quick test cut. mara repeated that because one person had asked whether the rule was different for turning soft wood.
- the small bandsaw has a new blade, but its fence has not been checked for square yet. nobody was asked to use it before that check.

we spent a while on the offcut rule because the bin label had disappeared. ben said that short pieces were useful for testing stain colors, and he had kept a shoebox of them under the finishing bench. mara said that was fine for labeled pieces, but the box could not become another unmarked pile. they did not decide on a new label design. someone suggested a yellow card, and leah wrote it on the back of the meeting sheet so it would not get lost before the next discussion.

after that, mara raised the saturday open-house table. the neighborhood association had asked whether the shop could bring a small display to its spring repair fair in april. the request was for examples of simple repairs, not for anyone to promise free work at the event. tom thought the shop could show a chair with a repaired rung and a drawer with a replaced runner. jo had a small stool that might be suitable, although she wanted to check whether its glue-up would be finished by then. the group did not commit to attending. mara said she would reply that the makerspace was considering it and ask how much table space was available.

there was also a brief conversation about the ventilation sign near the finishing corner. the sign says to keep the door closed while oil-based finishes are in use, but people sometimes prop it open when carrying in lumber. dev said he had noticed it wedged with a scrap of pine last week. leah said the door was heavy and the closer was slow, so a sign alone might not solve the problem. no one suggested changing the ventilation setup. they talked instead about putting a small doorstop in the office and taking it out only when lumber was being moved. mara was unsure whether that would be more confusing, and asked everyone to leave it as it was until they could discuss it with the building manager.

the meeting ended a little after seven forty. i stayed to put the chairs back, then watched ben test a finish sample on a piece of birch. he wrote “second coat?” on masking tape and stuck it beside the sample, rather than deciding right there whether it needed another coat. the sander was off by then, and the dust collector sounded quieter, though nobody had checked the motor. outside, the rain had stopped. i left with the cardboard rack template still on the table and the yellow-card suggestion written on the meeting sheet.", "output": "Last Thursday evening, I went to the Cedar Bench Workshop, a small woodworking makerspace in the old freight depot on Mason Street. I was there for the monthly member meeting, which started at six thirty in the room behind the tool library. A long maple board served as the meeting table, with a coffee ring near one end and a row of pencil marks that nobody seemed to mind.

Mara started with the usual shop update, but she had put a few things on paper because, as she said, “We keep having the same conversation and then forgetting which part we agreed to talk about.” The dust collector was running loudly again, mostly when the wide-belt sander was on. Tom had checked the outside vent and found a strip of loose mesh, but he had not opened the motor housing. Mara said she was not asking anyone to fix it during the meeting, only to decide who could look at it with her on Saturday. Dev volunteered, as long as they checked the manual first, since he had never worked on that model.

The next discussion was about the beginner bench area. Two new members had tried to use it on Monday and found the clamps mixed in with the hand planes. The room is narrow, so there was disagreement about whether a second rack would make things easier or leave too little walking space. Jo thought a wall rack could work beside the sharpening station, while Leah said that spot was already awkward when people carried long boards through. Nobody measured the space at the meeting. Instead, they agreed to take a tape measure and a piece of cardboard over there before ordering anything. Mara pointed out that this was a proposal, not a purchase decision.

1. Items people wanted to keep in view

- The cabinet key stays on the hook by the sign-in clipboard, rather than in the drawer where it had been found twice.
- The maple offcuts are for member projects, but anything shorter than six inches should go in the kindling bin unless someone labels it for a specific use.
- Safety glasses are still required at the lathe, even for a quick test cut. Mara repeated this because one person had asked whether the rule was different for turning soft wood.
- The small bandsaw has a new blade, but its fence has not yet been checked for square. Nobody was asked to use it before that check.

We spent a while discussing the offcut rule because the bin label had disappeared. Ben said short pieces were useful for testing stain colors and that he had kept a shoebox of them under the finishing bench. Mara said that was fine for labeled pieces, but the box could not become another unmarked pile. They did not decide on a new label design. Someone suggested a yellow card, and Leah wrote it on the back of the meeting sheet so the suggestion would not get lost before the next discussion.

After that, Mara raised the Saturday open-house table. The neighborhood association had asked whether the shop could bring a small display to its spring repair fair in April. The request was for examples of simple repairs, not for anyone to promise free work at the event. Tom thought the shop could show a chair with a repaired rung and a drawer with a replaced runner. Jo had a small stool that might be suitable, although she wanted to check whether its glue-up would be finished by then. The group did not commit to attending. Mara said she would reply that the makerspace was considering it and ask how much table space was available.

There was also a brief conversation about the ventilation sign near the finishing corner. It says to keep the door closed while oil-based finishes are in use, but people sometimes prop it open when carrying in lumber. Dev said he had noticed it wedged with a scrap of pine last week. Leah said the door was heavy and the closer was slow, so a sign alone might not solve the problem. No one suggested changing the ventilation setup. Instead, they discussed putting a small doorstop in the office and taking it out only when lumber was being moved. Mara was unsure whether that would be more confusing and asked everyone to leave things as they were until they could discuss it with the building manager.

He wrote “second coat?” on masking tape and stuck it beside the sample rather than deciding right then whether it needed another coat. The sander was off by then, and the dust collector sounded quieter, though nobody had checked the motor. Outside, the rain had stopped. I left with the cardboard rack template still on the table and the yellow-card suggestion written on the meeting sheet."}]
